sections.html:
Hamilton County is rural, with farmland, small towns and an estimated 14,799 residents. Jasper is the county seat, and the municipalities of Jennings and White Springs also levy tax. The county sits at the crossroads of I-75 and I-10, so buyers can come from Jacksonville, Gainesville or Tallahassee, and your bill depends on whether the parcel is inside a town.

The county has a moratorium on single-site RV and camper living, and no electric permits are issued for RVs. If the property you plan to sell has an RV hookup, ask the county before you list.

Each of three offices owns one step. The appraiser sets value and exemptions, the collector bills and collects, and the clerk runs the value adjustment board and tax deed sales.

  • Property appraiser: values every parcel, keeps the exemption rolls, and handles name, address and legal description changes. Call or visit the office in Jasper before March 1 to file for homestead.
  • Tax collector: online at hamiltontaxcollector.com, with a parcel search and online payment.
  • Clerk and value adjustment board: 207 NE 1st Street, Room 106, Jasper, phone 386-792-1288.
  • County commission: sets the county millage rate and handles questions such as the RV rule above.

Phone before you drive in, since county offices keep their own hours. Bring your parcel number or a copy of your last bill, which lets staff find your account quickly and answer questions about what is owed.

The collector lists rates in decimal form. Compare them with your TRIM notice and November bill.

Only one town line applies to a parcel. A rural parcel carries the county, school and water lines, while a house in Jasper adds the Jasper line. Non-ad valorem assessments are separate flat charges for services such as fire or solid waste, and they print on the same bill.

Millage is one dollar per thousand dollars of taxable value, so each line shows how much one body adds. Appraisal is the value, assessment is the tax owed, and the tax lien dates from January 1 of the tax year, which is why a bill can follow a house across a sale.

Statements are mailed by November 1. Payers get 4 percent off in November, then 3, 2 and 1 percent in the following three months. March is full price, and on April 1 the bill goes late. Real estate tax then takes a 3 percent penalty and the parcel is listed in the local paper from May on. Unpaid business property accrues 1.5 percent monthly.

Liens on unpaid real estate are sold online at the end of May or on June 1. Earlier in the year come the January 1 valuation date, the March 1 exemption cutoff and the August TRIM notice. A value petition is due 25 days after the TRIM notice.

You petition the value adjustment board through the clerk. The board decides only whether property is appraised at fair market value and whether an agricultural classification or exemption should be approved. It cannot lower a value because you cannot afford the tax, and it has no say over rates.

  • The filing fee is $15, and $5 more for each extra parcel when contiguous parcels are combined on one petition.
  • If the property appraiser or tax collector denied a timely homestead exemption or homestead tax deferral, there is no fee.
  • Petitions need an original signature, and copies or faxes are not accepted.
  • A late petition is sent to the board attorney, and a hearing is set only for good cause.

Talk to the property appraiser before filing; the clerk encourages it. The form is DR-486, and a postmark by the deadline does not save a petition that arrives late.

Homestead is the main one. File by March 1; it applies only to your permanent residence, so a rental or second home does not qualify. The first layer of the exemption is limited to $25,000, and a second layer can reach up to $25,000 more, school taxes excluded.

Owners with limited income can seek a deferral under Form DR-570, with the application due at the tax collector by March 31. When you sell, the cap that protected your old assessed value disappears, which is why the buyer's bill is often higher than yours. If you are moving to another Florida home, ask the property appraiser there about carrying part of the cap forward.

sections.h2: If a property goes to a tax deed sale
sections.html:
Once a certificate holder files an application, the clerk conducts the auction. Every property sells buyer beware and as is, with no promises on title, zoning, access or physical condition. The high bidder's nonrefundable cost deposit is set by s. 197.542(2).

A holder may apply two years after April 1 of the issue year, and homestead land opens at the taxes due plus half its latest assessed value. Paying the collector before the sale takes the parcel off the block. If your house has an advertised date, plan the sale of the home around it.

A little work up front keeps the sale smooth. Look up your parcel on the collector's site and note the amount due and the year it covers. Make sure the mailing address on file is current, because a bill sent to an old address still carries the same dates. Check that your name and legal description match your deed.

If you rent the property or run a business there, ask the appraiser whether a separate personal property account exists. Then decide whether you would rather pay the bill now or have it paid from the proceeds at closing. Either works, and the title agent will show it on the settlement statement. Keep a copy of the paid receipt or payoff letter with your closing papers in case a question comes up later.

Tell the closing agent about each unpaid year at the start. The agent gets a payoff from the collector and pays it from the sale proceeds, so you do not need cash in hand. Plan the timing around April 1, because the 3 percent penalty and the newspaper charge raise the payoff.

Ask for a draft settlement statement before the closing date and check that every tax line matches the collector's figure. Bring photo ID, your deed and your latest bill to the title agent, and confirm where your proceeds will be sent. Buyers who pay cash can often meet a tight schedule, a useful option when a certificate or sale date is near.

faqs.q: When does a Hamilton County bill go late?
faqs.a: On April 1. The collector adds a 3 percent penalty to real estate tax on that date and lists the parcel in the paper beginning in May.

faqs.q: How much is the Hamilton County early payment discount?
faqs.a: It starts at 4 percent for November and falls one point each month through February.

faqs.q: What does it cost to petition the Hamilton County value board?
faqs.a: $15, plus $5 for each added contiguous parcel. Petitions over a denied homestead or homestead deferral request have no fee.

faqs.q: Can a house with a tax certificate be sold in Hamilton County?
faqs.a: Yes. Closing pays the collector, the lien clears, and the buyer gets clean title. Ask for a payoff figure that includes interest.

faqs.q: Who decides the rate on my Hamilton County bill?
faqs.a: The taxing bodies decide, such as the county, school board, towns and the river district. The appraiser only sets value and handles exemptions.
